claims.text: A hybrid CALPHAD and machine-learning-corrected MTP workflow can accurately predict melting temperature and entropy of fusion for HEAs with at least five elements.
High-throughput CALPHAD can screen multicomponent alloys for solidus temperature and solid-solution stability.
The target space includes equimolar or near-equimolar alloys containing three to six refractory or transition-metal principal elements.
Increasing the number of principal elements tends to favor intermetallic-containing systems over disordered solid solutions.
Neural Evolution Structure generators can generate structures containing more than 40,000 atoms for the candidate alloys.
An MTP trained on a sparse DFT dataset can capture local lattice distortion and short-range order in high-entropy configurations.
MTP-based molecular dynamics and thermodynamic integration can determine solid-liquid free-energy differences, melting temperature, and entropy of fusion for these HEAs.
The simulations span temperatures from cryogenic conditions to above the solidus, reaching 3600 °C.
Configurational entropy proportional to ln(N) competes with favorable formation enthalpies of particular elemental pairs.
Atomic-size and electronic-structure mismatch among principal elements produces severe local lattice distortion and short-range order.
Local lattice distortion and short-range order stabilize the solid solution against intermetallic formation at high temperature.
Local lattice distortion and short-range order complicate the free-energy landscape.
Standard DFT is computationally prohibitive for supercells large enough to sample configurational entropy in alloys with at least five elements.
CALPHAD solidus predictions become unreliable when assessed binary interaction parameters for high-melting refractory pairs are missing or unreliable.
MTP represents the relevant nonlinear local-environment effects with near-DFT accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost.
The workflow will attain an error below 1 meV per atom relative to DFT benchmarks.
The workflow will predict experimental melting properties with less than 5% deviation.
Alloys containing favorable Nb-W interactions will have higher melting temperatures than simple linear mixing rules predict.
CALPHAD calculations restricted to assessed binary databases fail for more than 95% of systems containing at least five elements because of missing data.

The method is principally valid for equimolar or near-equimolar, solid-solution-dominant alloys and may lose accuracy when non-equimolar compositions undergo phase separation or complex intermetallic precipitation not represented in training.
